summary.text: Fix \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and choose a prime \(p\) beyond both the alleged threshold and \(e^4\). For prime \(p\), the only admissible integers are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)=2\), while \(p>e^4\) implies \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\), contradicting the lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ divides }n\}.
\]
We disprove the assertion that, for every \(\epsilon>0\), one has
\[
a(n)\ge (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\).

The key observation is that \(a(n)\) is bounded along the infinite subsequence of prime numbers. More precisely, we first prove that
\[
a(p)=2
\]
for every prime \(p\).

Indeed, the set of prime factors of \(p\) is the singleton \(\{p\}\). Both \(1\) and \(p\) are counted by \(a(p)\): the integer \(1\) has no prime factors, so its set of prime factors is the empty set and is therefore a subset of \(\{p\}\); and the only prime factor of \(p\) is \(p\) itself.

Conversely, suppose that \(k\) is counted by \(a(p)\). Thus
\[
1\le k\le p
\]
and every prime factor of \(k\) belongs to \(\{p\}\). If \(k=1\), this is one of the two integers already listed. If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has at least one prime divisor; let \(q\) be such a divisor. Since every prime factor of \(k\) must be a prime factor of \(p\), we have \(q=p\). Hence \(p\mid k\), and therefore \(p\le k\). Combining this with \(k\le p\) gives \(k=p\). Thus no integers other than \(1\) and \(p\) are counted, proving \(a(p)=2\).

Now choose the particular positive value
\[
\epsilon=\frac12.
\]
If the conjectured statement were true, there would be some threshold \(N\in\mathbb N\) such that every integer \(n\ge N\) satisfies
\[
(\log n)^{1-1/2}=(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).
\]

There are arbitrarily large primes. Consequently, we may choose a prime \(p\) which is at least \(N\) and is also strictly larger than \(e^4\). For example, choose a prime at least
\[
\max\bigl(N,\lceil e^4\rceil+1\bigr).
\]
Then \(p\ge N\), so the asserted eventual lower bound applies to \(p\). On the other hand, because the logarithm is strictly increasing on the positive real numbers and \(p>e^4\),
\[
\log p>\log(e^4)=4.
\]
In particular \(\log p>0\), and taking nonnegative square roots yields
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}=\sqrt{\log p}>\sqrt4=2.
\]
But \(p\) is prime, so the result proved above gives \(a(p)=2\). Therefore
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}>2=a(p),
\]
whereas the conjectured lower bound at this same \(p\ge N\) requires
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)=2.
\]
This is a contradiction.

Hence the proposed statement is false: already for \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\), no threshold can make \(a(n)\ge(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\) hold for every sufficiently large \(n\). The infinitely many prime inputs, on which \(a(p)=2\), provide arbitrarily large counterexamples.
